hints: Start with what you actually see after the run - separate coloured spots at different heights above the baseline. What two distances could you measure for each spot?
Think about how to make the position of a spot into a standard number that is the same even if the solvent runs further on another day. What ratio links pigment movement to solvent movement?
Once you have a number for each unknown spot, how would you use published data or known samples run alongside to put a name to each pigment?
walkthrough:
See Separation As A Starting Point**
You are sitting beside the chromatogram. Each pigment has moved a different distance because of its different solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper. So you have coloured spots separated by height. To identify them you need to turn position into a comparable value.

Turn Distance Into Rf**
Measure from the baseline (origin line) to the centre of each pigment spot, and from the baseline to the solvent front. Then calculate: $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by pigment from baseline}}{\text{distance moved by solvent from baseline}}$$ This ratio is constant for a given pigment in a given solvent system, so it removes differences in run time or length.

Match To Identify**
Compare each calculated $R_f$ with known, standard or table $R_f$ values for chloroplast pigments, or with spots of known pigments run at the same time. A match identifies the pigment.

Final answer: Calculate $R_f$ value for each pigment spot where $R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by pigment from baseline}}{\text{distance moved by solvent from baseline}}$; compare calculated values with known / standard / table values to identify pigments.

hints: Remember chlorophyll a in the reaction centre can only absorb certain wavelengths well. What problem does that leave for the plant in white light?
Think of carotene and xanthophyll as helpers around the reaction centre. What extra job could they do with light before chlorophyll a acts?
After absorbing that extra light, what must happen to the energy so it can still be used for photochemistry in the reaction centre?
walkthrough:
Why Helpers Are Needed**
Chlorophyll a in the reaction centre is the molecule that actually loses an electron when excited, but it absorbs mainly red and blue light. That leaves a gap in the middle of the spectrum. Carotene (orange) and xanthophyll (yellow) fill that gap.

Harvest Extra Light**
These two pigments are called accessory pigments. They absorb wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll a / the reaction centre / primary pigment. This extends the range of wavelengths that can be harvested for photosynthesis, so more of white light is useful.

Funnel Energy To The Centre**
They do not drive photochemistry themselves. They pass the absorbed energy on to the reaction centre chlorophyll a, which then becomes excited and passes an electron to the electron transport chain.

Final answer: Carotene and xanthophyll are accessory pigments; absorb light wavelengths not absorbed by reaction centre / primary pigment / chlorophyll a, so extend range of wavelengths absorbed; pass energy to reaction centre / chlorophyll a for photosynthesis.

hints: Start in the stroma where carbon dioxide enters the cycle. What 5-carbon acceptor must carbon dioxide join onto first?
Think about the enzyme that makes this joining possible and the name given to this first step of making organic carbon from inorganic carbon.
The first 6-carbon product is very unstable. How many carbons will each of the two molecules it splits into have?
Those 3-carbon acids must then be made more energetic using products from the light-dependent stage. Which two molecules provide energy and reducing power?
The reduced 3-carbon product sits at a branch point. What must happen to most of it so the cycle can keep turning?
What can the remaining small amount of that 3-carbon product be used to build, from sugars to other organic molecules?
Pull it together - what is the overall name of this cyclic pathway in the stroma?
walkthrough:
Fix Carbon Dioxide To RuBP**
In the stroma, carbon dioxide reacts and combines with the 5-carbon acceptor ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP. This is catalysed by the enzyme rubisco. This step is called carbon fixation because inorganic carbon dioxide is now fixed into an organic molecule. It is the start of the Calvin cycle.

Split The Unstable 6-Carbon Intermediate**
The 6-carbon compound formed is unstable and immediately breaks down to form two molecules of the 3-carbon compound glycerate 3-phosphate, GP.

Reduce GP To TP Using Light Products**
Each GP is then reduced to triose phosphate, TP. This needs energy and hydrogen from the light-dependent stage: ATP supplies energy and reduced NADP supplies reducing power (hydrogen and electrons). This is why the light-independent stage still depends on light indirectly.

Regenerate The Acceptor And Build Useful Products**
Most TP is recycled to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue to fix more carbon dioxide. This regeneration also uses ATP. Only a small proportion of TP is taken out to make useful organic products such as hexoses, sucrose, starch, cellulose, glycerol and lipids, and amino acids from GP.

Keep The Big Picture**
No light is needed directly, but ATP and reduced NADP must be continuously supplied. The cycle turns to net-produce TP while maintaining the RuBP pool.

Final answer: In Calvin cycle in stroma: carbon dioxide combines with ribulose bisphosphate / RuBP catalysed by rubisco - carbon fixation; forms unstable 6C compound which splits to 2 x glycerate 3-phosphate / GP; GP reduced to triose phosphate / TP using ATP and reduced NADP from light-dependent stage; most TP used to regenerate RuBP; remainder used to form hexoses / sucrose / starch / cellulose / lipids / amino acids etc.
